scenes.spec: heat-shimmer parking lot, driver gets in, vents blast — hand held to vent, disappointment
scenes.narration: First real hot day of the year. You crank the AC, hold your hand to the vent, and get... air. Moving air, sure. Cold? Not really. Maybe cool-ish after ten minutes on the highway, maybe cold on one side and warm on the other, maybe just a fan doing cardio. Car AC isn't magic and it isn't a black box — it's a loop that moves heat from inside your car to outside it, and it fails in ranked, recognizable ways. And one PSA up front this episode will keep repeating: the parts-store recharge can is both the cheapest fix on this list and the most expensive mistake, depending on one question almost nobody asks first.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
three-way split — "Not cold at all / cool-not-cold" / "Cold sometimes (moving vs idle)" / "One side cold, one warm"
scenes.narration: **Version one: never really cold.** Blows fine, temperature wrong. The classic low-refrigerant story — but "low" MEANS "leaked," hold that thought. **Version two: cold on the highway, warm at idle** — or cold mornings, warm afternoons. Heat-rejection problem: condenser or its fan, usually. **Version three: driver's side arctic, passenger side Sahara** (or vice versa). Almost always a **blend door** — a cabin airflow flap — not a refrigerant problem at all. Dual-zone cars are full of these. And one more datum: does the AC button click the compressor on? Listen for the under-hood click-and-RPM-dip when you press it. No click = the system is refusing to engage, which is itself a diagnosis. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the listen-for-the-click check]

scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — THE LOOP IN NINETY SECONDS
scenes.spec: NEW 3D — AC loop: compressor squeezes refrigerant hot → condenser (front of car) dumps heat outside → expansion device drops pressure → evaporator (in dash) gets COLD → cabin air blows across it → back to compressor; phase-change color coding
scenes.narration: Ninety seconds of honest physics: refrigerant is a fluid chosen because it boils at useful temperatures. The **compressor** squeezes it hot; the **condenser** (the radiator-looking thing up front) dumps that heat to outside air; the **expansion device** lets the pressure crash, which makes the refrigerant *very cold*; the **evaporator** (a small radiator inside your dash) gets cold with it; your blower pushes cabin air across it — cold vents. Loop repeats. So cold air needs: enough refrigerant, a working squeezer, heat actually leaving at the condenser, and cabin air actually routed across the cold core. Four requirements. Four failure families.

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — LOW REFRIGERANT, WHICH MEANS A LEAK (the ep-6 rule returns)
scenes.spec: loop with level dropping — leak points glowing: hose crimps, O-rings, condenser stone-strike, evaporator; UV dye glow
scenes.narration: Same law as coolant, same phrasing on purpose: **the AC loop is sealed — refrigerant doesn't get used up, it escapes.** A system that needs a "recharge" every spring has a leak renting space in it. Common exits: rubber-line crimps and O-rings, a condenser holed by road debris, or the evaporator aging out behind the dash (tell: the drain sometimes stops dripping and the cabin smells vaguely sweet-chemical). Shops find leaks with UV dye — same trick as the oil episode — or an electronic sniffer. [TECH CONFIRM — your top AC leak sites by frequency; condenser stone-strikes common?] **The recharge-can PSA, part one:** a can on a leaky system is renting cold by the month while venting refrigerant — which is both money and (depending on refrigerant) not something to shrug at environmentally. Leak-test first is the honest sequence. [TECH CONFIRM — your counter-speech version; also R-134a vs R-1234yf cost reality — the newer refrigerant changed recharge economics a LOT, worth numbers]

scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — COMPRESSOR AND CLUTCH (the no-click and the racket)
scenes.spec: compressor — clutch face engaging/not; seized internals; metal debris path through loop
scenes.narration: The squeezer fails two ways. Quietly: the **clutch** never engages (no click) — sometimes just a low-refrigerant lockout protecting itself, sometimes electrical, sometimes the clutch itself. Loudly: bearing racket, rattles, or a compressor that grenades internally and — the expensive sentence — sends metal debris through the whole loop, which is why a proper compressor replacement includes flushing and often a new condenser/dryer. The "cheap compressor swap" that skips the flush is a repeat customer generator. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the full-service-not-just-the-part framing; how often do you see debris- contaminated systems from prior cheap swaps?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #3 — HEAT REJECTION: CONDENSER AIRFLOW AND FANS (the at-idle pattern)
scenes.spec: condenser airflow — highway ram air vs idle fan dependence; fins packed with bugs/plastic bag; fan dead
scenes.narration: Version-two symptoms live here: cold while moving, warm at idle means the condenser only sheds heat with ram air — its **fan** isn't pulling (same fan story as the overheating episode; the systems share hardware on many cars) or its fins are packed with bugs, cottonwood fluff, or the classic plastic shopping bag. A garden-hose fin rinse (gentle, straight-on) is legitimate owner maintenance. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the fin-rinse advice with your cautions]

scenes.section: CAUSE #4 — CABIN AIRFLOW: BLEND DOORS, CABIN FILTER, AND THE MOLDY CORE
scenes.spec: dash airflow — blend door actuator clicking/stuck half-open; cabin filter black with debris; evaporator core furred
scenes.narration: Refrigerant loop perfect, cabin plumbing wrong: **blend door actuators** (little motors aiming flaps) fail with a signature *click-click-click behind the dash* and cause the one-side-warm split or heat stuck on. A **choked cabin filter** — the filter everyone forgets exists — strangles total airflow so even cold air arrives weak. And a furred, moldy **evaporator** smells gym-sock and blocks flow. Cabin filter is glovebox-DIY on most cars; check yours today. [TECH CONFIRM — blend-door actuator failures: which symptom do you see most? Cabin filter neglect stories?]

scenes.section: THE REPAIR — WHAT THE MONEY LOOKS LIKE
scenes.spec: decision path — performance test → leak test → targeted fix; NOT can-first
scenes.narration: The honest sequence at a shop: **performance test** (vent temps, pressures on gauges — the pressures tell a story to a trained eye) → **leak identification** → targeted repair → evacuate, recharge by WEIGHT (not by can-feel), verify. scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Comfort tier" / "Book it" / "Shut it off"
scenes.narration: **Comfort tier:** most of this episode. An AC that's merely warm strands nobody — fix it when the calendar and wallet agree. (Exception carve-out: heat waves are genuinely dangerous for kids, elders, and long commutes — comfort-tier doesn't mean trivial.) **Book it:** the every-spring-recharge pattern (that's a leak on a payment plan), at-idle warmth (fan issues also threaten engine cooling — ep 5 cousin), or any compressor noise. **Shut it off:** grinding/rattling from the compressor area, or AC engagement that stalls or screeches the engine. Running a dying compressor is how a part becomes a whole-loop contamination job. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers]

So: cold air is a loop doing four jobs, and the failure pattern names the job — never-cold says leak, idle-warm says airflow outside, one-side-warm says a flap inside, and no-click says the system is protecting itself or refusing. The recharge can without a leak test is renting cold; the gauge-and-dye visit is buying it back. And check that cabin filter — today, seriously, it's three minutes. Next time, the season finale: a little red battery icon lights up while you're driving — and you have a surprisingly short, surprisingly calm window to do the exact right thing.
